name: Clarivex
description: Clarivex is a selective adenosine-antagonist and dopaminergic modulator designed to produce sustained, tunnel-vision focus for 6-8 hours. It works by suppressing default-mode network activity while potentiating prefrontal executive function, effectively eliminating mind-wandering, emotional intrusion, and sensory distraction. The standard prescription form of the corporate workday.
effects: Complete suppression of distraction and mind-wandering
Enhanced sustained attention on single task
Reduction of emotional interference with cognitive tasks
side_effects: Social blunting — difficulty reading interpersonal cues while active
Long-term: reduced baseline focus capacity without drug
cultural_context: Clarivex is the quintessential corporate drug — so normalized in Tier 3-4 office environments that not taking it is seen as unprofessional or a sign of cognitive inadequacy. Analysts, data architects, and BCI-linked project managers run on it. The drug's emotional flatness during dosing has contributed to a documented increase in workplace depersonalization syndromes. On the Shelf, stolen or counterfeit Clarivex (street name 'Glass') is used by students in Tier 2 community academies who can't afford Lazarus pricing.
story_hooks: A Tier 4 analyst realizes she hasn't felt an authentic emotion during work hours in three years — every breakthrough, every crisis, every loss processed through Clarivex's emotional filter. She's been promoted twice and doesn't know who she is anymore.

A batch of counterfeit 'Glass' circulating through Tier 2 schools contains a dopamine cascade agent — students are becoming violently fixated on whatever they were doing when they dosed, unable to disengage for days.
A Lazarus whistleblower has data showing Clarivex's long-term focus-dependency effect was known during trials and suppressed — the drug was designed to create its own market.
